newsitem.title: USA: Clinton firm on limiting NATO expansion to three.
newsitem.headline: Clinton firm on limiting NATO expansion to three.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday dug in his heels on limiting expansion of NATO to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic for now, rejecting a French-led clamour to include Romania and Slovenia as well.

"I don't want to exclude anyone but I think it quite important on principle that we not admit anyone until we're absolutely sure that their democracy is stable and that they are militarily capable," Clinton said in an interview with broadcasters from Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Spain.

Clinton, who leaves late on Friday for next week's NATO summit in Madrid, said Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic were currently the only countries "that can start tomorrow and within a reasonable time meet the same standards of membership militarily that the other NATO countries met."

"I don't forsee any circumstances under which I would change my position that today we ought to have three," Clinton said. His unyielding posture suggested next week's meeting of leaders of the Western alliance could be a fractious affair.

A French government statement on Wednesday contradicted Washington, saying five former communist East European countries were qualified to join an enlarged NATO, not just the three the United States wants to admit. The statement was issued after conservative President Jacques Chirac discussed the issue with Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin.

Since NATO operates by consensus, Clinton's insistence on three seemed likely to prevail at the July 8-9 summit. But French Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux said on Thursday: "There is no consensus on three, four or five."

Clinton was also at odds with France on its demand that the United States hand over NATO's southern command, which controls the Mediterranean, to the Europeans. France has made this the price for rejoining the integrated military structure it quit in 1966 under then President Charles de Gaulle.

In the interview, Clinton said relinquishing this command, known in NATO parlance as AFSOUTH, "wouldn't, from our point of view, be a sensible thing to do militarily" because the U.S. Sixth Fleet is its major element.
"Except for, and maybe even including ... our presence in South Korea, it's the biggest single deployment of United States military assets anywhere," Clinton said.

Clinton and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton were to fly first to Majorca to be guests of King Juan Carlos and Queen Sofia of Spain at a Moorish castle. They will go to Madrid on Monday for the two-day summit, which opens the next day.
The president planned to visit Poland on Thursday and Romania on Friday before going to Denmark for a state visit.
In preparation for the trip, Clinton met with his national security advisers on Thursday morning and held an afternoon ceremony with leaders of 34 military veterans groups who back NATO enlargement.
Joseph Frank, national commander of the American Legion, the largest veteran's group, said enlarging the alliance was "a major step forward for the security of Europe."

While NATO expansion has stirred little public debate in the United States so far, many members of the foreign policy establishment are against it, including such disparate individuals as former Defence Secretary Robert McNamara and former Secretary of State Henry Kissinger.

They argue that expansion will tend to destabilise Europe by antagonizing Russia and creating envy among former Soviet bloc states that are excluded from the 48-year-old alliance, which was conceived as a bulwark against Moscow.
The Pentagon has estimated expansion will cost U.S. taxpayers $150 million to $200 million a year over the next 10 years.

A poll conducted by the Pew Research Foundation indicated the U.S. public is almost evenly split on whether NATO should take in new members. Forty-three percent favoured expansion, while 41 percent wanted the alliance to stay as is.

The survey of 1,206 adults, conducted on April 3-6, found that 14 percent had no opinion on expansion and 2 percent wanted NATO eliminated. The poll found substantial support for a larger NATO among the 6 percent of Americans who follow the issue closely. Sixty-one percent of them favoured expansion.
